cards.title: Founder Ad = Founder's Argument, Not Raw Footage
cards.summary: A founder ad is a structured presentation of the founder's argument across three story elements, not simply video of the founder talking.
cards.use_when: Planning a founder-led ad concept for a Meta acquisition campaign and deciding what the ad actually needs to communicate.
steps: Treat the founder ad as a constructed argument rather than documentary footage of the founder. The source defines it as a structured presentation of the founder's case, not just a camera pointed at them.

Build the argument from three elements: the origin (why the business started), the unique mechanism (why the solution works, explained by the founder or an expert), and an adversarial angle (tearing down competitors or industry norms).
Anchor the origin to a real problem the founder encountered that maps to the customer's problem — this is what makes the authority credible rather than decorative.
Use the unique mechanism to explain why the product works differently, giving the founder or an expert the role of explaining the mechanism.
Use the adversarial angle to differentiate: name what the industry does wrong and position the product against it.
This framework suits founder-led brands where the founder has genuine category authority or a credible origin story. If the founder has neither, a witness or proxy format may fit better.
caveats: The source frames this as a definition and architecture, not a guaranteed performance formula; adversarial claims should be truthful and substantiated.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Highest-Performing Founder Script Structure
cards.summary: The source's strongest founder script sequence runs Claim, Proof of Claim, Unique Mechanism tied to founder story, Proof of Mechanism, CTA plus social proof.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing the body script for a founder-led video ad before shooting.
steps: Open with an adversarial claim that challenges the viewer's assumptions about the category (the source's example: 'the industry is lying to you'). This creates tension before the product is introduced.
Immediately provide proof of that claim so the adversarial opening reads as credible rather than inflammatory.
Introduce the unique mechanism tied to the founder's story — connect why the product works to why the founder built it.
Back the mechanism with proof of mechanism: evidence, demonstration, or results that validate the explanation.
End with a clear CTA plus social proof to close the loop on trust.
Run this as the body script, then test multiple hooks in front of it rather than rewriting the whole structure per concept.
caveats: This is presented as the source's highest-performing founder structure, not a universal law; it depends on having a real adversarial claim and real proof to back it.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Hooks Should Target Viewer Desire, Not Founder Narrative
cards.summary: Effective hooks speak to the viewer's underlying desire or problem; hooks that only narrate the founder's personal story underperform.
cards.use_when: Writing hook variants for a founder video ad or diagnosing why a founder ad has weak thumb-stop rate.
steps: Write hooks around the viewer's underlying desire or problem first, not around the founder's personal journey. The founder's story belongs in the body, not the opening line.
Keep the body script stable and swap the hook to isolate the variable being tested. One body can carry several hooks.
Test two to four hook variations per body script. Going much wider spreads the testing budget too thin to read a result.
Evaluate hooks against the specific stage of awareness the ad targets — the same claim lands differently on problem-unaware versus solution-aware viewers.
If a founder ad is underperforming on retention, check whether the opening is narrating the founder rather than the viewer's problem before rewriting the body.
caveats: The two-to-four hook range is the source's testing heuristic, not a calculated threshold; adjust based on available spend and volume.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Batch-Shoot Modular Creative for Volume
cards.summary: Pair many hooks with a few core body scripts to scale creative volume efficiently from a single shoot day.
cards.use_when: Planning a founder video shoot and deciding how many assets to produce per session.
steps: Break the creative into modular components: hooks and bodies shot as separate units.
Use the source's arithmetic as a planning model: 10 hooks × 3 bodies = 30 ads.
Shoot all hooks in one batch against the same lighting and setup, then shoot the three body scripts separately.
In editing, assemble each hook with each body to produce the full matrix of ad variations.
Continue swapping hooks as results come in without re-shooting bodies, which keeps marginal creative cost low.
This approach suits founder-led brands that can get the founder on camera for a limited window; the shoot is planned around component coverage rather than finished ads.
caveats: Volume of combinations is not the same as volume of distinct concepts; the source pairs this with concept diversification so the matrix is not just cosmetic variation.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Concept Diversification via Founder Script Roles
cards.summary: Move the founder out of the standard first-person protagonist role into witness, interviewer, or reader roles to create genuinely different ad concepts.
cards.use_when: Your founder ads all feel the same and you need distinct concepts without changing the offer or product.
steps: Default founder ads use the protagonist role: first-person, founder speaking directly about their own story.

Diversify by changing the founder's script role: the witness (founder reads a customer email or message aloud), the interviewer (founder questions the lab or product team), and the reader (founder reads a one-star review).
Each role changes the emotional entry point and the credibility mechanism without changing the product or offer.
Treat role changes as concept-level variation, not hook-level variation — they should feel like different ads, not edits of the same ad.
Match the role to the stage of awareness: a reader-of-a-bad-review format suits skeptical audiences, an interviewer format suits audiences who want mechanism proof.
Distinguish this from superficial variation such as set or wardrobe changes when assessing whether the concept is truly different.
caveats: Reads or reviews used in the witness or reader formats should be real and permission-appropriate; fabricated testimonials create legal and trust risk.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: The Founder Involvement Spectrum
cards.summary: Vary how much of the founder appears — from full protagonist to completely absent — to extend creative range and reduce format fatigue.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to involve the founder in the next creative batch, especially when shoot time or talent budget is limited.
steps: Place each creative on a spectrum of founder involvement rather than defaulting to full face-and-voice delivery.
Protagonist: the founder on camera speaking in first person — highest authority, highest production demand.
Voice: the founder narrates over product or b-roll rather than appearing on camera.
Evidence: the founder appears indirectly, for example photos of the founder in the lab or facility.
Proxy: an employee or other trusted person tells the founder's story on camera.
Absent: no founder at all, told through animation or other formats.
Use the spectrum to book shoot time efficiently — a single session can yield protagonist, voice, and evidence assets.
Rotate across the spectrum to avoid format fatigue in the account without abandoning founder authority entirely.
caveats: Lower involvement generally means weaker direct founder authority; the source presents the spectrum as range, not as a claim that outcomes are equal across levels.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Editing Dynamics to Avoid Format Fatigue
cards.summary: Vary camera angles, scenery, and edit dynamics across founder videos so repeated exposure does not fatigue the format.
cards.use_when: Founder videos are still running but performance is declining and you need to refresh without changing the core concept.
steps: Introduce dynamic editing: multiple camera angles within a single video rather than one static talking-head shot.
Change scenery and setting across different ads in the same concept family so they do not read as identical.
Combine low-fi, UGC-style footage with high-end product shots to keep a premium brand positioning intact while retaining the authenticity of founder content.
Use editing variation as a cheaper refresh lever than re-shooting; it can extend the life of existing footage.
Track which combinations of angle, scenery, and edit style are running and rotate them instead of repeating the same edit across all placements.
caveats: This reduces format fatigue; it does not fix a weak hook or a missing argument. Pair it with hook and concept variation.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx

cards.title: Match Founder Ads to Stage of Awareness
cards.summary: Founder content should be built for a specific stage of awareness, and the claim, mechanism, and proof mix should shift accordingly.
cards.use_when: Mapping a founder ad set to cold versus warm audiences or diagnosing why a founder ad works in one placement but not another.
steps: Decide which stage of awareness each founder ad targets before scripting, since the same founder story does not land identically at every stage.
For less aware audiences, lead with the problem and the adversarial claim so the viewer recognizes the problem before the product appears.
For more aware audiences, the unique mechanism and proof of mechanism can carry more of the runtime, since the problem is already established.
Reuse the same founder story assets across stages by altering which element is emphasized in the hook and opening, rather than rebuilding from scratch.
Keep the target stage explicit in the creative brief so editors and media buyers are aligned on which asset belongs to which audience.
caveats: The source identifies targeting specific stages of awareness as a component of founder ad performance; it does not provide numeric suppression or frequency rules.
cards.source_name: How To Create Founder Ads That Scale (Masterclass).docx
